clips.text: Your body is 60% water — and fewer than 100 people on Earth are allergic to it.
Hold on to this picture — skin, breaking out in red hives, from nothing but a drop of plain water.
In the next nine minutes: the shower you cannot take, the rain on your commute, your own sweat turning on you, the 1964 laboratory, and the question at the end — what would you give up first?
You wake up, and the first thing you do is the thing you cannot do. You stand in front of the shower, hand on the tap, and you do not turn it on. For you, a hot shower is a rash waiting to happen.

It is only water. Clear, clean, ordinary water. The same water you drank yesterday, the same water falling on the roof right now. For about ten seconds, you think your skin is overreacting. It is not.
Within twenty minutes, the hives arrive — red, raised, burning welts, exactly where the water touched you. Not everywhere. Only where the drops landed, like a map of the rain itself.

Fewer than one hundred people in the world live like this — fewer than a hundred cases ever reported in the medical literature. And the reason starts with something you do every morning without thinking. That is the rain.

Chapter two: the rain. You step outside, umbrella up, hood up, and the city does not care. A bus splashes a puddle across your legs. A drip finds the gap at your collar. Every drop is an appointment with your own skin.
Rain on your skin is not refreshing. It stings, then it itches, then the hives bloom — each drop a small red island, spreading until your forearm looks like a map of somewhere painful.

Doctors call it aquagenic urticaria — hives brought on by water. A 2017 review found only thirty-seven cases since 1964. A later review puts the total at around one hundred. Either way, it is one of the rarest conditions a dermatologist will ever see.

The pattern is almost polite. The hives appear within twenty to thirty minutes of contact, and fade within thirty to sixty. No swelling of the throat, no closing airway — just your skin, protesting water, and then forgiving it.
And here is the part that sounds impossible: most patients can still drink water. The reaction is on the skin only. A glass of water goes down fine. It is the outside of you that cannot stand it.
So the water you drink is safe, and the water that touches you is not. The difference is your skin — and what it does with water is where this story gets strange. That is the sweat.
Chapter three: the workout. You lace up your shoes, you start to run, and ten minutes in, your own body turns on you. Because sweat is water too — and your skin does not know the difference.

Your own sweat breaks you out. The harder you run, the worse it gets — hives blooming across your back and chest, as if your body were allergic to its own effort. The workout that should make you feel alive attacks your skin.

Remember the number: your body is about sixty percent water. Blood, sweat, tears, saliva — all of it water, all of it you. The substance you are made of is the one your skin cannot tolerate from the outside.
Tears count too. So does saliva. A sad film, a yawn, a kiss — any of it can set the hives off. Your body is not just reacting to the weather. It is reacting to itself.
The mechanism has four moves. First: the contact. Water touches your skin, and something in the skin's natural oils — the sebum — reacts with it, forming a substance that should not be there.
Second: the signal. That substance acts like a histamine liberator — a chemical key that tells the mast cells in your skin to open up and dump histamine, the same chemical behind a nettle sting.
Third: the hives. The histamine makes the tiny blood vessels under your skin leak a little fluid, and the skin swells into red, raised welts — exactly where the water touched, nowhere else.
Fourth: the mystery. Nobody has ever proven the sebum theory. It is the leading hypothesis from 1964, and sixty years later, the true cause is still unknown. That is the evening.
Chapter four: the evening. You are on the sofa, watching a sad film, and the tears come — and with them, the hives. The cruelest twist is not the rain. It is that your own feelings can set it off.
You cry, and your cheeks break out. Not from the film. From the tears themselves — salt water, your own salt water, running down your own face and raising hives in its path.
Think about what that means. Every emotion that makes you cry — grief, joy, a wedding, a goodbye — comes with a price on your skin. The body that feels everything cannot even weep in peace.

Tessa Hansen-Smith, from California, has lived with this since she was eight. She showers twice a month. Her tears, her sweat, her saliva — all of them break her out. In the most severe cases, even drinking water burns.
Rachel Warwick, in Britain, showers once a week — and plans her whole life around it. The washing, the swimming, the rainy days other people barely notice: every one of them is a negotiation.
Two women, two lives built around avoiding water. And yet neither of them is allergic in the way you think — because this is not a true allergy at all. That is the laboratory.
Chapter five: the laboratory. In 1964, two doctors in America, Shelley and Rawnsley, met a patient whose skin broke out after a swim — and they tested the water itself.

They tried everything. Tap water, distilled water, sea water, rain water — every kind raised the hives. Temperature did not matter. It was the water itself. That was the first clue, and it is still the biggest one.

In 1981, another team showed the histamine release directly: during water exposure, the mast cells dumped histamine, the chemical behind the swelling and the itch. The mechanism was real, even if the trigger was not understood.

And here is the honest part: the cause is genuinely unknown. The sebum theory is a hypothesis, not a proven fact. It affects women more often, and usually starts at puberty — and nobody knows why either.
The record has four marks. First: 1964 — Shelley and Rawnsley describe the first case in the Journal of the American Medical Association, and propose the sebum theory.
Second: 1981 — Sibbald and his colleagues demonstrate the histamine release during water exposure, proving the mast cells in the skin are doing the damage.
Third: 2017 — a review of the literature counts only thirty-seven cases in more than fifty years. The condition is so rare that most dermatologists will never see a single patient with it.

Fourth: 2020 — a new review puts the total at around one hundred cases, and reports a teenage girl helped by omalizumab after antihistamines failed. One case. Not a cure. Not a pattern. Just a door, slightly open. That is the test.
Chapter six: the test. You have dodged the shower, the rain, your sweat, your tears. Now the choice is yours: if you could give up one thing to keep the rest, what would it be?
Would you give up the hot shower — the steam, the warmth, the ten quiet minutes at the start of the day? Or the swim — the cold shock of a lake in summer, the weightless feeling of floating?
There is no cure. Antihistamines help many patients — the same pills you take for hay fever — but they only soften the reaction, they do not stop it. And for some people, even they are not enough.

Omalizumab helped one reported case — a teenage girl, whose hives would not answer to antihistamines, who improved on monthly injections and stayed well for two years. One case. It is hope, not a treatment.
So here is the question the story turns on: if your body turned against water tomorrow — the rain, the shower, your own sweat — what is the first thing you would miss, and could you live without it?
There is no right answer. There is only the answer you would give — and that answer says something about how much of your life is made of water. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.

Chapter seven: today. You still shower in the morning, still walk in the rain, still sweat at the gym. Nothing about you has changed — except now you know there are people for whom each of those is a negotiation.
Remember the numbers: about sixty percent of you is water, fewer than one hundred cases ever reported, hives in twenty to thirty minutes, gone in thirty to sixty.

And remember the twist: most patients can still drink water. The thing you are made of does not poison you from the inside — it only attacks from the outside, through the skin. The enemy was never the water.
If you were allergic to water — what's the first thing you'd miss: a hot shower, a swim, or a rainy day? Tell us why.

Science note, plainly: the case count varies by source, so say fewer than one hundred reported cases, never a precise census; the cause is unknown and the sebum theory is only a hypothesis; most patients can drink water; there is no cure, and omalizumab helped one case only; and this is not medical advice.

The named studies, so you can check me: Shelley and Rawnsley, 1964, in the Journal of the American Medical Association; Robles-Tenorio and colleagues, 2020; and the omalizumab case, BMJ Case Reports, 2022.

Your body is sixty percent water — and fewer than one hundred people on Earth are allergic to it. The next time it rains, you will step outside without thinking. Now you know what that freedom is worth.
